passage: By the time Esther's aunt came out to the courtyard with the washing basket, the skipping rope lay in the dust and both children were talking at once. "She grabbed it when it was my go!" "He was holding it for ages, he always keeps it!" "You never let anyone finish a turn!" "You always cry when you lose!" Abebe's voice climbed higher with every sentence. Esther didn't even look at him; she was counting on her fingers all the times he had cheated at games last month. The aunt set down the basket. "Wait. What happened first?" Neither answered the question. Each was already opening their mouth to add one more thing the other had done.

qa.q: What were the children arguing over in the courtyard?
qa.a: They were arguing over the skipping rope, which lay in the dust.

qa.q: How was Esther feeling as she counted on her fingers instead of looking at Abebe?
qa.a: She was resentful and set on winning, collecting all the times she thought he had cheated last month instead of listening to him.

qa.q: What could the aunt try so the argument does not climb any higher?
qa.a: She could ask each child to tell their side one at a time while the other only listens, and repeat back what she heard before anyone replies.

qa.q: What is it like for Abebe when Esther won't even look at him?
qa.a: Abebe probably feels unheard, which may be why his voice keeps climbing; he is shouting to be noticed as much as to win.

grounding: Shows two children each telling the story so only the other is to blame, trading 'always' and 'never' while nobody listens.

passage: In the corridor outside the Class 5 staff room, Wasim and Devika stood by the water cooler, both red in the face. The cricket bat between them had a crack along the handle. "Devika threw it on the ground after her turn, Ma'am, I saw!" "No, Wasim hit the wall with it! You always blame me for everything." "And you never admit anything!" Mrs Kulkarni, the games teacher, opened her mouth, but Wasim was already talking again, listing every broken thing from last term. Devika wasn't listening; her lips were moving as she got her next answer ready. Neither of them looked at the bat anymore. It had become a contest over who would get the last word.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cricket bat?
qa.a: The cricket bat had a crack along the handle.

qa.q: How was Devika feeling as her lips moved?
qa.a: She felt defensive and set on winning, red in the face and getting her next answer ready instead of listening to Wasim.

qa.q: How could Mrs Kulkarni turn this moment around?
qa.a: She could set the bat aside, ask both children to drink some water, and give each a turn to speak without interruption before deciding anything.

qa.q: If you were Mrs Kulkarni, what would you notice about the argument?
qa.a: The teacher would notice that neither child looks at the bat anymore; the fight is now only about getting the last word.

grounding: Shows two children in a school corridor each blaming the other with 'always' and 'never', too busy preparing defences to listen.
